source_system.method: Source-linked technique evidence selected from reviewed public actor profiles.

provenance_model.mapping_unit: One actor, campaign and procedure claim mapped to the most specific defensible ATT&CK technique.
provenance_model.known_limit: The compact publication layer preserves normalized procedure statements and links, not verbatim source excerpts or private analyst notes. Readers must review the cited source before reusing a claim.

behaviours.name: Phishing
behaviours.summary: A branching educational model for phishing operations that may pursue credentials, access tokens or code execution. It describes plausible relationships, not a mandatory sequence or a claim about a specific incident.
behaviours.boundary: The model intentionally stops after initial credential or payload outcomes. Persistence, discovery, lateral movement and collection depend on the operator, objective and access obtained and must be supported separately.

branches.name: Preparation
branches.description: Infrastructure that may be acquired before delivery. Many campaigns instead use compromised or legitimate services.

branches.name: Delivery
branches.description: How the lure reaches the target.

branches.name: Credential and token theft
branches.description: The link ends at a collection or authorisation workflow rather than malware execution.

branches.name: Payload execution
branches.description: The user action or client exploit leads to code execution or retrieval of a follow-on payload.

techniques.notes: An operator may register a lookalike or campaign domain for a lure, credential portal, redirector or payload host.
techniques.caveat: Phishing can use compromised domains, legitimate services or direct attachments, so domain acquisition is not required.

sources.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains — T1583.001

techniques.notes: Common web services may support lure delivery, redirects, payload staging or later command channels.
techniques.caveat: Use of a public service is not malicious by itself and does not identify an operator.

sources.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services — T1583.006

techniques.notes: The message carries an attachment intended to produce access, execution or further user interaction.
techniques.caveat: An attachment may be benign-looking and contain only a link; map the actual delivery and execution evidence.

sources.title: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment — T1566.001

techniques.notes: The lure contains a link that may lead to credential theft, token abuse, a malicious download or client exploitation.
techniques.caveat: A clicked link does not establish which downstream branch occurred.

sources.title: Phishing: Spearphishing Link — T1566.002

techniques.notes: The lure is delivered through a third-party service such as personal email, social media or another messaging platform.
techniques.caveat: The service is a delivery channel, not evidence that the service provider or account owner operates the campaign.

sources.title: Phishing: Spearphishing via Service — T1566.003

techniques.notes: A fraudulent login portal may collect credentials entered by the victim.
techniques.caveat: A cloned login page supports this branch only when form behaviour, collection endpoints or telemetry show input capture.

sources.title: Input Capture: Web Portal Capture — T1056.003

techniques.notes: Consent or device-code phishing may produce an application token without collecting a reusable password.
techniques.caveat: A phishing URL alone does not prove token issuance; authorisation and identity-provider evidence are needed.

sources.title: Steal Application Access Token — T1528

techniques.notes: The victim follows a link that contributes to code execution, a download or another execution chain.
techniques.caveat: Credential-only phishing may involve a click without producing code execution on the endpoint.

sources.title: User Execution: Malicious Link — T1204.001

techniques.notes: The victim opens or executes a malicious attachment or downloaded file.
techniques.caveat: Delivery of a file does not prove it was opened, executed or successful.

sources.title: User Execution: Malicious File — T1204.002

techniques.notes: A link or attachment may exploit a vulnerability in a browser, document reader or other client application.
techniques.caveat: Most phishing does not require a software vulnerability; do not infer exploitation from a crash or suspicious file alone.

sources.title: Exploitation for Client Execution — T1203

techniques.notes: A successful payload branch may invoke PowerShell for execution, retrieval or post-compromise actions.
techniques.caveat: PowerShell is one possible interpreter and is neither universal to phishing nor malicious by itself.

sources.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell — T1059.001

techniques.technique: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
techniques.notes: A document, script file or downloaded stage may use Visual Basic or VBA for execution.
techniques.caveat: The file type and code path must be inspected; an Office attachment alone does not establish this technique.

sources.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic — T1059.005

techniques.notes: A lure or downloaded component may use JavaScript or JScript to execute the next stage.
techniques.caveat: JavaScript on a landing page is normal; evidence must distinguish ordinary web code from an execution mechanism.

sources.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript/JScript — T1059.007

techniques.notes: An initial script or loader may retrieve an additional payload from external infrastructure.
techniques.caveat: A download following a click is not automatically an adversary tool transfer; preserve process, network and file evidence.

sources.title: Ingress Tool Transfer — T1105
